Its automated fire-control system calculates lead angles to improve hit probability and reduce ammunition expenditure. The Ka-52M has an advantage in poor weather, with its advanced Rezets active electronically scanned array (AESA) radar providing better resolution for detecting small drones against ground clutter than the Mi-28's N025 radar. headline: Boeing has delivered the 22nd F-15EX Eagle II to the U.S. Air Force, and the aircraft is the first F-15EX destined for permanent assignment to the 67th Fighter Squadron at Kadena Air Base, Japan. The aircraft departed Boeing's St. Louis facility on August 28 and is currently at Portland Air National Guard Base, Oregon, where it will receive additional preparation before eventually moving to Kadena. The first permanently stationed F-15EXs are expected to begin arriving at Kadena during fiscal year 2027, which begins October 1st. The Air Force has said the F-15EX will bring advanced avionics, enhanced survivability, modern electronic-warfare systems and increased weapons capacity to Kadena, while the transition period is intended to give Airmen experience operating and sustaining the aircraft before it becomes a permanent part of the wing. Kadena is ultimately planned to receive 36 F-15EXs to replace its aging F-15C/D fleet.

headline: Newsweek reports that the USS Abraham Lincoln will make another port stop before returning to the United States, extending a deployment that has already lasted 286 days. The carrier was originally expected home in early summer but was diverted from the IndoPacific to the Middle East in January to support U.S. operations during the Iran war. A family member of a Lincoln sailor told Newsweek that the additional stop is needed because the carrier still has to fulfill time originally assigned to the IndoPacific after being diverted. The Navy has not independently confirmed that explanation, and Newsweek notes that multiple port visits during a carrier's return phase are not unusual and can serve maintenance, logistical, diplomatic and crew welfare purposes. Publicly available Navy material also does not establish that carriers must “make up” a fixed number of days after a diversion. The Lincoln arrived in Thailand on Sept. 2 after approximately 250 days without a port visit, allowing roughly 5,000 sailors and Marines to go ashore. The Navy says the carrier will return as part of a planned rotation, while congressional lawmakers have raised questions about the deployment's effect on service member well being, maintenance schedules and fleet readiness. Source: https://www.newsweek.com/uss-abraham-lincoln-thailand-port-stop-heading-home-explainer-12402308 Photo: https://www.thainewspix.com/en/preview/55512

headline: Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum announced that excavation work is set to begin for the Great Triumphal Arch and Military Observation Deck at Memorial Circle on Columbia Island, between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Burgum says the project fulfills a vision that dates back more than 125 years. The 1902 McMillan Commission called for a monumental treatment at the western terminus of Arlington Memorial Bridge, while the 1924 Arlington Memorial Bridge Commission described Columbia Island as an appropriate site for a formal park and plaza connecting the bridge with Arlington Cemetery. According to Burgum, the site instead became a largely undeveloped traffic circle. The planned arch is intended to provide the monumental treatment envisioned in those earlier plans, with Burgum describing it as a major work of American architecture honoring the history and significance of Arlington National Cemetery. He also noted that Washington, D.C., is unusual among major Western capitals in lacking a major triumphal arch.

headline: Military Times reports that a federal appeals court has restored Bowe Bergdahl’s 2017 court martial conviction, overturning a 2023 decision that vacated it. A three judge D.C. Circuit panel ruled that the civilian district court did not have jurisdiction to overturn the military judgment, saying collateral review of court martial convictions must remain within the military justice system. Bergdahl pleaded guilty in 2017 to desertion and misbehavior before the enemy after walking away from his Afghanistan post in 2009 and being captured by the Taliban. The search for him resulted in severe injuries to other U.S. troops and the death of a military working dog. He was dishonorably discharged and ordered to forfeit $10,000 in pay, but received no prison sentence after presenting evidence of torture and abuse in captivity. The 2023 ruling had vacated the conviction after finding that the military judge had failed to disclose an application for an executive-branch immigration judge position, potentially creating a conflict of interest. Bergdahl’s attorneys also argued that Donald Trump’s public calls for Bergdahl to be severely punished, including a call for execution during the 2016 campaign, created improper command influence. The appeals court did not rule on either of those underlying issues. Bergdahl’s attorney says the case still raises serious questions about the integrity of the military justice system, and his legal team has 45 days to consider seeking reconsideration or Supreme Court review. Source: https://www.militarytimes.com/news/your-military/2026/09/03/court-overturns-2023-ruling-that-wiped-bowe-bergdahls-conviction/

Instead, personnel were told to use broader language such as “overseas operations in the CENTCOM Area of Responsibility.” The guidance reportedly went beyond the Air Force and was disseminated across the Defense Department. Trump formally notified Congress on July 7 that U.S. military action against Iran had restarted after the April ceasefire collapsed. The timing has also created questions about casualty accounting. Four service members killed in July were initially categorized by the Defense Department as killed during Operation Epic Fury, despite the Pentagon now saying the operation ended May 5. They were subsequently moved into a new “overseas operations” category, reducing the recorded Epic Fury deaths from 18 to 14. The Pentagon attributed the earlier classification to a “temporary data disruption,” while the current casualty system still contains apparent inconsistencies, including June wounded and a July death listed under Epic Fury. The broader issue is that the Pentagon now acknowledges a May 5 end date that it previously declined to provide publicly, even though U.S. and Iranian forces continued exchanging fire and U.S. military operations related to the conflict continued afterward.
